title: Cache adoption elasticity and cost-savings sensitivity (workbook draft)
content:
Purpose:
This workbook draft explores how customer adoption curves for prefix/KV caching and transient warm-up behavior change realized hit rates over short and medium horizons, and what that implies for per-token unit economics. Focus is on realistic rollouts (canary -> ramp -> full), segment-level adoption elasticity, and how short-lived bursts and churn hurt forward-looking savings estimates.

High-level questions we want answers to:
- For a typical mid-market app (1M monthly queries), what near-term savings can we promise after a 30/60/90 day rollout if adoption follows a logistic ramp?
- How sensitive are savings to (a) initial adoption (b) retention/churn of cached prefixes (c) TTLs and prefetch windows?
- Where are the operational risks (cache pollution, quality regressions) that materially cut the theoretical savings?

Assumptions (baseline):
- Baseline token cost (no cache): $0.012 per 1k input+output tokens.
- Average tokens per request: 120 tokens.
- Requests per month (baseline segment): 1,000,000.
- Baseline cost/month = 1,000,000 * 120 / 1000 * $0.012 = $1,440.
- Prefix cache only reduces model tokens on average by 35% for covered requests; KV-cache (full response reuse) reduces by 90% for exact matches.
- Warmup penalty: first N requests after cache miss incur 50% higher latency and no hit savings until warmed (modeled as extra tokens or lost hits depending on approach).
- Adoption curve model: logistic growth parameterized by initial adoption A0, growth rate r, inflection at day t0.

Scenario table (sample rows exported from sheet):
Scenario ID,Segment,Monthly Requests,Prefix Hit %,KV Hit %,Effective Hit %,Cost w/o cache,Cost w/ cache,Savings $,Savings % ,Notes
S1,Early adopter app,1,000,000,20,5,0.26,$1,440,$1,072,$368,25.6,"A0=10%, r=0.07/day, t0=20d; TTL=24h; shallow prefetch"
S2,PLG mid-market,1,000,000,35,8,0.43,$1,440,$838,$602,41.8,"A0=20%, r=0.05/day, t0=35d; TTL=72h; aggressive KV suggestions"
S3,Enterprise-heavy,1,000,000,50,15,0.65,$1,440,$504,$936,65.0,"A0=40%, r=0.03/day, t0=60d; longer TTLs, lower churn"
S4,High-churn-burst,1,000,000,15,2,0.17,$1,440,$1,232,$208,14.4,"Burst traffic w/ 60% unique prefixes; warmup loss modeled as 10% hit erosion"

Notes on calculations (how Effective Hit % computed):
- Effective Hit % = PrefixHit + (1 - PrefixHit) * KVHit * KVMatchQualityAdjustment - WarmupErosion
- KVMatchQualityAdjustment defaults to 0.9 (not all KV hits avoid model work fully due to partial reuse).
- WarmupErosion approximates lost hits from transient cold-starts; calibrated to observed traffic skew.
- Cost w/ cache = BaselineCost * (1 - EffectiveHit% * AverageReductionPerHit) where AverageReductionPerHit is weighted by prefix vs KV reductions (prefix=0.35, kv=0.9).

Sensitivity sweep (exported pivot rows):
- Vary initial adoption A0 in {5%,10%,20%,40%} with fixed r=0.05,t0=30d. After 90 days cumulative savings range from 8% -> 52% depending on A0.
- Vary TTL in {6h,24h,72h,7d}: shorter TTLs reduce steady-state hit-rate by ~12–28% for high-churn segments.
- Warmup penalty from 0% -> 20% hit erosion causes savings to drop nonlinearly; most sensitive when middle-of-the-road adoption (20–35%).

Break-even and payback heuristic (for Dedicated / Reserved capacity tradeoffs):
- If expected steady-state savings > 30% and monthly baseline > $5k, recommend considering reserved capacity sizing exercises.
- Payback window (purchase dedicated capacity to lower per-token base by 25%) computed as: UpfrontCommit / MonthlySavings. Example: $30k commit to reduce per-token cost from $0.012 -> $0.009 yields breakeven in ~5 months for a 1M request/month mid-market with effective 40% hit rate.

Operational caveats and observed pitfalls (from field sampling):
- Cold-start churn: mobile/social apps with many unique prompts see hit fragmentation; need prefetch strategies and client-side shaping to reduce entropy.
- Cache pollution: naive KV suggestions can push high-entropy tokens into cache unless we score by long-term qualifier (session stability).
- Quality regressions: prefix rewrites and normalization can improve hit-rate but may change model outputs enough to break product assumptions — include eval gate.
- Instrumentation gaps: token-level attribution (per-route, per-client) is incomplete in ~30% of sampled accounts which biases hit-rate estimates upward.

Recommendations (next actions):
- Short-term (2–4 weeks): build a small A/B experiment harness to test A0 uplift from a lightweight client opt-in (goal: +10–15% adoption in week1). Capture token-level telemetry and TTL-decay. Owner: Marcus.
- Medium-term (1–3 months): run a TTL sweep across 20 customers to quantify steady-state hit elasticity. Implement prefetch for top-5 prefixes per customer. Owner: Lena.
- Product changes: add a cache-quality score in Console that shows expected reduction in tokens per route and a confidence band (low/med/high) so solutions can triage rollout risk.
- Modeling: incorporate churn-aware Monte Carlo (sampled prefix churn) into the existing cost-model to avoid optimistic steady-state assumptions. Owner: Elliot.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to standardize prefix normalization heuristics across models without changing semantic outputs? (design spike)
- What is an acceptable degradation threshold for product owners when cache normalization increases hit rates? (ops SLA + eval)
- Need a small privacy review for client-side prefetch hints (possible PII leakage).

Appendix (export snippets):
- Example logistic adoption function used in simulations: A(t) = Amax / (1 + exp(-r*(t - t0))) ; Amax capped at 0.9 to model never-perfect adoption.
- Quick sanity check: for S2 numbers (EffectiveHit 43%), monthly tokens saved = 1,000,000 * 120 * 0.43 = 51,960,000 tokens -> cost saved at $0.012/1k = $623.52. Our spreadsheet adjusts that by hit mix and partial reductions to reach $602 shown above.
